```{r setup}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(stringr)
library(forcats); library(ggplot2); library(scales); library(knitr)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
theme_update(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot",
             plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey45", hjust = 0))
BLUE <- "#1b4965"; LIGHT <- "#9cc3d5"

fisc  <- read_csv("data_clean/fiscal_outturn.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cats  <- read_csv("data_clean/findings_by_category_tidy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
paras <- read_csv("data_clean/unresolved_paragraphs.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
obs   <- read_csv("data_clean/notable_observations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(headline_amount = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(headline_amount)))

# Human-friendly money formatter
money <- function(v, cur) {
  ifelse(is.na(v), "not stated",
  ifelse(cur == "USD",
    ifelse(v >= 1e6, paste0("US$", comma(v/1e6, accuracy = 0.1), " million"),
                     paste0("US$", comma(v, accuracy = 1))),
    ifelse(v >= 1e9, paste0("K", comma(v/1e9, accuracy = 0.01), " billion"),
    ifelse(v >= 1e6, paste0("K", comma(v/1e6, accuracy = 0.1), " million"),
                     paste0("K", comma(v, accuracy = 1))))))
}
short_min <- function(x) x |>
  str_replace("Ministry of ", "") |>
  str_replace("Office of the President - Provincial Administration", "Provincial offices") |>
  str_replace("Office of the Vice President \\(DMMU\\)", "Disaster unit (DMMU)")
```

> **What this is.** Every year, Zambia's Auditor General checks how the government collected and spent public money, and publishes a report. This page sums up five of those reports, for the years 2021 to 2025, in plain language. Every figure comes straight from the reports, and the page number is on record.
>
> **One thing to keep in mind.** An audit "finding" is a question the auditors could not close, not a proven crime. It means the records did not fully add up, or an explanation was still owed when the report was written. So read these as "money the government could not fully account for," not "money that was stolen."

# The short version

```{r headline}
f <- fisc |> filter(financial_year == 2025)
f22 <- fisc |> filter(financial_year == 2022)
tibble(
  " " = c(
    "Government planned to spend (2025)",
    "Government actually spent (2025)",
    "Left unspent against the plan (2025)",
    "Money collected minus money spent (surplus, 2025)",
    "Open audit questions (paragraphs) in 2025",
    "Open audit questions in 2022"),
  "Amount / figure" = c(
    money(f$final_budget_payments, "ZMW"),
    money(f$actual_payments, "ZMW"),
    money(f$final_budget_payments - f$actual_payments, "ZMW"),
    money(f$surplus_deficit, "ZMW"),
    "27",
    "40")) |> kable()
```

In short, over these five years:

- The government has been spending a **bigger share of its budget** than before: 76 out of every 100 Kwacha budgeted in 2022, rising to about 86 in 2025.
- Its **surplus has shrunk**, from about K30 billion in 2022 to about K2 billion in 2025. It is collecting and spending much closer to the line.
- The **number of unresolved audit questions has fallen**, from 40 in 2022 to 27 in 2025.
- But the **same ministries keep coming up** year after year, and the reports still list large sums that were not collected, not delivered, or not properly supported.

# How government money moved

Each report compares what the government **planned** to spend (the final budget) with what it **actually** spent.

```{r budget-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
fisc |> filter(!is.na(actual_payments)) |>
  select(financial_year, Planned = final_budget_payments, Spent = actual_payments) |>
  pivot_longer(-financial_year, names_to = "which", values_to = "k") |>
  mutate(which = factor(which, levels = c("Planned","Spent"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(financial_year), k/1e9, fill = which)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .7), width = .62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(k/1e9, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_dodge(width = .7), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Planned = LIGHT, Spent = BLUE)) +
  labs(title = "What government planned to spend vs what it spent",
       subtitle = "Kwacha, billions",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Auditor General, Statement B (budget execution), page 5 of each report. 2021 not reported.") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

In 2025 the government planned to spend about **K251 billion** and spent about **K216 billion**. The roughly **K34 billion** gap is money that was budgeted but not spent in the year. Under-spending is not automatically good or bad: it can mean careful restraint, but it can also mean projects ran late or expected funding did not arrive.

A **surplus** means the government collected more than it spent that year. That surplus has been getting smaller.

```{r surplus-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
fisc |> filter(!is.na(surplus_deficit)) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(financial_year), surplus_deficit/1e9)) +
  geom_col(fill = BLUE, width = .6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(surplus_deficit/1e9, accuracy = 0.1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) +
  labs(title = "Surplus: money collected minus money spent",
       subtitle = "Kwacha, billions",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Auditor General, Statement B, page 5 of each report.")
```

*(The 2021 report does not include this budget table, so 2021 is left out of this section.)*

# What the auditors flagged, and how much

When the auditors cannot fully account for money, they record it under a category, such as money not collected, irregular payments, or funds that were not properly supported by documents. The 2022 and 2023 reports add up these categories into a single table. Those are the only two years with a comparable total, so the trend below covers 2021 to 2023.

```{r findings-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
pick <- tibble(financial_year = c(2021L,2022L,2023L), report_year = c(2022L,2023L,2023L))
series <- cats |> inner_join(pick, by = c("financial_year","report_year")) |>
  mutate(arrears = str_detect(str_to_lower(category_printed), "tax arrears"))
series |> group_by(financial_year) |>
  summarise(`All findings` = sum(amount_kwacha, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Without the tax-arrears line` = sum(amount_kwacha[!arrears], na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-financial_year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "k") |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(financial_year), k/1e9, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .7), width = .62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comma(k/1e9, accuracy = .1)),
            position = position_dodge(width = .7), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("All findings" = BLUE, "Without the tax-arrears line" = LIGHT)) +
  labs(title = "Value of audit findings each year",
       subtitle = "Kwacha, billions",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Auditor General trend tables, 2022 and 2023 reports, page ii.") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

One line dwarfs all the others: **unpaid tax arrears**, which the tax authority (ZRA) reports separately and which runs into tens of billions of Kwacha. It is a running backlog of taxes owed, not money that went missing in the year. Once you set it aside (the lighter bars), the rest of the findings are far smaller, and they do not simply fall every year.

# Real examples: what was not collected, not delivered, or not supported

These are specific cases the reports single out. Amounts are exactly as the reports state them. Kwacha (K) and US dollar (US$) items are kept separate.

**Money the government was owed but did not collect:**

```{r cases-revenue}
obs |> filter(section == "Revenue", !is.na(headline_amount)) |>
  arrange(desc(financial_year), desc(headline_amount)) |>
  transmute(Year = financial_year,
            Ministry = short_min(ministry_std),
            `What the report records` = observation,
            Amount = money(headline_amount, currency),
            Page = paste0("p", source_pdf_page)) |>
  kable()
```

**Money spent, at risk, or not delivered:**

```{r cases-expenditure}
obs |> filter(section == "Expenditure", !is.na(headline_amount)) |>
  arrange(desc(financial_year), desc(headline_amount)) |>
  transmute(Year = financial_year,
            Ministry = short_min(ministry_std),
            `What the report records` = observation,
            Amount = money(headline_amount, currency),
            Page = paste0("p", source_pdf_page)) |>
  kable()
```

A few plain-language examples from the tables above:

- In 2024, farming inputs worth **K25.7 million** for the 2024/2025 season were **not delivered** to the farmers they were meant for.
- In 2025, the Ministry of Health owed **K3.56 billion** in unpaid bills, some dating back to 2014.
- In 2025, fines of **K626.6 million** imposed by the Mines Ministry had **not been collected**.
- In 2021, the government paid **US$7.8 million** towards a business jet that was never delivered, out of a US$49.4 million contract.
- In 2021, oxygen cylinders were bought uncompetitively for **US$13 million**, without checking other suppliers.

These are the kinds of cases behind the headline totals. Each one is a question the auditors raised, not a proven loss.

# Which ministries come up most often

The reports are organised by ministry. Counting how often each one appears with an unresolved question is a fair way to see who recurs, even where no single total is given.

```{r recurrence-chart}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
paras |> group_by(ministry_std) |>
  summarise(years = n_distinct(financial_year), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(years == 5) |>
  mutate(name = short_min(ministry_std), name = fct_reorder(name, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, name)) +
  geom_col(fill = BLUE) + geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.3, size = 3.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .1))) +
  labs(title = "Ministries flagged in every report, 2021 to 2025",
       subtitle = "Number of unresolved-finding sections over the five years",
       x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "Source: Auditor General, contents pages. A count of sections, not an amount of money.")
```

Nine portfolios appear in **every** report over the five years. Provincial offices under the Office of the President come up most, followed by Finance, Agriculture, Home Affairs, Education, and Health. This points to where problems recur, but it does not by itself say which ministry lost the most money.

# How to read these numbers fairly

- **A finding is a question, not a verdict.** Say "the report records K3.56 billion in unpaid obligations," not "the ministry lost K3.56 billion."
- **Not every year lines up.** The budget table is missing for 2021; the single findings total exists only for 2022 and 2023; the 2024 and 2025 reports list examples instead of one total.
- **One huge line (tax arrears) distorts the totals**, so it is shown separately.
- **US dollar and Kwacha amounts are never added together.**
- **Counting how often a ministry appears is not the same as how much money is involved.**
- These figures come from the published main reports only. Ministries may have since given explanations, which later reports and parliamentary committees record.

# Where this comes from

Five reports from the Office of the Auditor General of Zambia, *Reports on the Accounts of the Republic*, for the years ended 31 December 2021 to 2025. Cite any figure with the report year and the page shown here, for example *Auditor General, 2025 report, page 5.*

The full data, the page references for every number, and the code that produced each chart are in the project repository: **https://github.com/Chanza-bj/AG_Report_Analysis**
